sections.h2: Who bills property tax in Dearborn, Michigan?
sections.html:
The City of Dearborn bills and collects property tax on Dearborn parcels, and Wayne County is the county the city sits in. The Treasury Division takes payments at the Dearborn Administrative Center, 16901 Michigan Avenue, with the cashier's counter open Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

The city's Assessing Department, in Suite 5 of the same building, values every parcel each year. Its phone is 313-943-2140 and the hours are 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. on weekdays. It answers email and voicemail within 48 hours and no later than seven business days, according to the city's assessing page.

Deeds are not recorded in Dearborn. The Wayne County Register of Deeds, on the sixth floor of the International Building at 400 Monroe in Detroit, holds deeds, and the city's assessing page points owners there for copies and for liber and page numbers.

sections.h2: When are Dearborn property taxes due?
sections.html:
Dearborn bills twice a year. Summer taxes are levied on July 1 and due September 14, and winter taxes are levied on December 1 and due February 14.

Dearborn tax bills and their due dates, from the city's treasury page
BillLeviedDueWhat it covers
SummerJuly 1Sept. 14, or in installments Sept. 14, Nov. 14 and Jan. 14School tax, city tax and the county-allocated operating tax
WinterDec. 1Feb. 14, paid in fullRemainder of county taxes and the city's Combined Sewer Overflow debt

Paying summer tax in installments carries a one-time $3 fee. Eligible residents may apply to defer summer tax. Winter tax has no installment option.

The city does not accept a postmark as proof of payment. A payment is posted on the day Dearborn receives it, so mail early or use the 24-hour secure drop box in the parking lot across from the main doors of the Administrative Center.

sections.h2: How can I pay a Dearborn tax bill?
sections.html:
You can pay online, by mobile app, in person, by mail, or by automatic bank debit. The method changes what you pay in fees.

  • Online through the BS&A site is free to owners who register their parcel, but a debit or credit card adds a 3% convenience fee and an e-check adds $3. An occupant who is not the owner pays $6 to open an account.
  • The DivDat app and the kiosk in the Administrative Center entrance charge 3% on cards, and e-checks through the app are free.
  • Mailed checks go to City of Dearborn, Tax Dept. 3102, P.O. Box 30516, Lansing, MI 48909-8016, with the account and parcel numbers on the check. Certified mail must go to the Administrative Center instead.
  • Automatic ACH debit from a bank account is free and can be cancelled at any time.

A seller who is closing near a due date should ask the title company to pay from proceeds by a method that posts the same day.

sections.h2: How does Dearborn assess a house, and why does a sale change the bill?
sections.html:
Dearborn sets the assessed value of a home at 50% of its estimated market value. Taxes equal taxable value divided by 1,000 and multiplied by the millage rate, a formula the State of Michigan sets for every city and township.

Since Proposal A in 1994, taxable value on an existing owner's home can rise each year only by inflation or 5%, whichever is less. That cap lifts in the year after a transfer of ownership, when taxable value resets to assessed value. A house that sells at $220,000 would be assessed near $110,000, and a buyer's first bill can be well above what the seller paid.

Sellers should understand this before listing a long-held property. The new owner's tax estimate is based on the uncapped figure, not on the seller's bill. The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 figures give Dearborn a median owner-occupied home value of $218,800, and 68.4% of its occupied homes are owner-occupied.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Dearborn assessment or claim an exemption?
sections.html:
Start with the Assessing Department, because many disputes are misread facts that can be corrected at the counter. If that does not settle it, appeal to the March Board of Review, which the city says is the only time of year an owner can contest value, and only for the current year.

Bring photographs, appraisals or comparable sales and a completed Board of Review petition. Residential owners who lose there can petition the Michigan Tax Tribunal, and residential property must go through the March board first. Commercial and industrial parcels may skip that step.

  • Principal Residence Exemption: removes the local school operating tax, up to 18 mills, on an owner-occupied home.
  • Poverty exemption: grants relief at 50% of value under MCL 211.7u, and the application and documents must be in by the last December Board of Review meeting.
  • Disabled veterans exemption: affidavit Form 5107 is filed after January 1 and before December 31, and VA proof is required.

sections.h2: What paperwork follows a Dearborn home sale?
sections.html:
Both the buyer and the seller owe the assessor paperwork. The new owner must file a Property Transfer Affidavit within 45 days of the transfer, and a late filing costs $5 per day up to $200 on residential property.

A seller who claimed the principal residence exemption files a Request to Rescind Principal Residence Exemption, Form 2602, with an effective date equal to the closing date. A buyer who will live in the house files Form 2368 to claim the exemption, plus a Name and Address Change form. The affidavit is required even when no deed is recorded.

Ask the Wayne County Treasurer, and the Dearborn Treasury Division, for the exact payoff on any unpaid bill before closing. Delinquency penalties, interest and the point at which collection moves from the city to the county are details to confirm with those offices rather than assume.

sections.h2: What should a Dearborn seller know about the local housing base?
sections.html:
Dearborn is an inner-ring suburb that borders Detroit on the north and east, roughly seven miles west of downtown Detroit. It became a city in 1927, and a 1928 vote merged Dearborn with neighboring Fordson. The Ford Motor Company world headquarters and the River Rouge Complex are here, and the city also has a University of Michigan campus and Henry Ford College.

The 2020 census counted 109,976 residents, and the Census Bureau estimates 105,611 for July 2025, a fall of 4.0%. The city covers 24.25 square miles at about 4,536 people per square mile, so lots are compact. Households average 2.92 people, 30.3% of residents were born abroad, and 53.4% of people age 5 and over speak a language other than English at home.

Median household income is $65,324, median gross rent is $1,327, and median monthly owner costs are $1,672 with a mortgage and $764 without one. Poverty runs 24.3%. A seller with an older house should expect a buyer to ask for roof, plumbing and electrical records, and the Assessing Department's record cards can be viewed during business hours.

faqs.q: When is Dearborn summer tax due?
faqs.a: Summer tax is due September 14. It may be paid in three installments on September 14, November 14 and January 14, with a one-time $3 fee for splitting it.

faqs.q: Can I pay Dearborn winter tax in installments?
faqs.a: No. Winter tax, levied December 1, is due in full by February 14 with no installment option.

faqs.q: Does a postmark count as paying on time in Dearborn?
faqs.a: No. The city does not accept postmarks, and a mailed payment is posted on the day Dearborn receives it. A 24-hour drop box sits in the Administrative Center parking lot.

faqs.q: How do I appeal my Dearborn assessment?
faqs.a: Call the Assessing Department first, then petition the March Board of Review. A residential owner who still disagrees can go to the Michigan Tax Tribunal.

faqs.q: Do I file anything with the city after buying a house in Dearborn?
faqs.a: Yes. Within 45 days the new owner files a Property Transfer Affidavit with the assessor, and a buyer who will occupy the house can file Form 2368 for the principal residence exemption.
